title: Task 12 - Jenkins-Docker Continuous Deployment
prereq: Docker Desktop, Jenkins and the registry running (`cd deploy\jenkins; docker compose up -d`), and at least one successful build of the job that deployed to staging (it was build #12 in this recording, started live in the Task 8 video).
The admin password is read from deploy/jenkins/.env by the commands; never show that file.
Port 8081 is the staging environment (prod is 8082).

recovery.symptom: The registry answers nothing on port 5000
recovery.fix: `docker ps --filter name=registry`; start it with `cd deploy\jenkins; docker compose up -d`. If the Task 3 demo server is still running on 5000, stop it first.

recovery.symptom: staging containers are not running / port 8081 does not answer
recovery.fix: Run the Jenkins job once more (Build with Parameters, APP_ENV=staging) or `cd` to the repo and start the stack with the tag of the last build: `$env:IMAGE_PREFIX='localhost:5000/'; $env:IMAGE_TAG='1.1.0-<commit>'; $env:HOST_PORT='8081'; $env:SECRET_KEY='<any long text>'; docker compose -p hotel-staging up -d --no-build`.
The JENKINS_ADMIN_PASSWORD line in deploy/jenkins/.env is wrong. Use the one Jenkins was first started with.

recovery.symptom: The tag in the video does not match yours
recovery.fix: Your last build has another commit. The commands compute the tag from the last build's name, so use them unchanged.

extra.what: List every published release (these are the rollback candidates)

extraQuestions.a: No. Publishing to Docker Hub is implemented (REGISTRY=docker.io/<id> plus the Jenkins credential registry-creds) but was never run, because it needs a Docker Hub account and an access token. A local registry, registry:2 on port 5000, was used and tested. Nothing was published externally and no registry credential is stored in the repository.

extraQuestions.q: How do you know the container is running exactly the image Jenkins tested and pushed?
extraQuestions.a: Three matching facts: the version-commit tag that the build computed, the image labels and /health that report the same version and commit, and the image ID of the running container, which equals the image ID of the tag in the registry. The pipeline's health stage also greps /health for the exact version and commit of this build.

extraQuestions.q: Was a fresh container created by this deployment?
extraQuestions.a: Yes: the Jenkins log shows 'Container hotel-staging-app-1 Recreate/Recreated' because the rebuilt image had a new image ID. Compose only recreates a container when its image or settings changed; the database stays in the named volume.

steps.title: From a tested commit to a deployed release: the last build
steps.say: This is Task 12, Jenkins and Docker continuous deployment. Continuous deployment means that every change that passes the tests is delivered automatically. Here is the proof from the build I started live in the previous video. The command reads the admin password from the environment file without showing it. The latest build is number twelve, named with the version and the commit, and the result is success. The stages show the quality gate: the tests come first, and the images are built, published and deployed only after them.
steps.cmd: $jh = @{ Authorization = 'Basic ' + [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes('admin:' + ((Get-Content deploy/jenkins/.env | Where-Object { $_ -like 'JENKINS_ADMIN_PASSWORD=*' }) -replace '^[^=]+=', ''))) }; $b = Invoke-RestMethod 'http://localhost:8090/job/hotel-booking/lastBuild/api/json?tree=number,displayName,result' -Headers $jh; $tag = $b.displayName -replace '^#\d+ ', ''; "last build: #$($b.number)   $($b.displayName)   $($b.result)"; (Invoke-RestMethod 'http://localhost:8090/job/hotel-booking/lastBuild/wfapi/describe' -Headers $jh).stages | Select-Object name, status | Format-Table -AutoSize
steps.expect: 'last build: #12   #12 1.1.0-1c2103c   SUCCESS' and the stages Checkout ... Unit & integration tests, E2E tests, Package source, Build images, Publish images, Deploy, Health check, all SUCCESS.
steps.tell: Only after the tests passed did the build create the images and deploy them.

steps.title: Versioned image tags: version plus commit SHA
steps.say: How is the release identified? The tag of every image is the version from the VERSION file, a dash, and the short commit id. Here are the three pieces: the version, the commit at the tip of develop, and the tag I compute from them, which is exactly the tag of the build. The Jenkinsfile builds it in the checkout stage. So the tag tells you which release and which commit an image contains.
steps.cmd: 'VERSION file   : ' + (Get-Content VERSION); 'commit (develop): ' + (git rev-parse --short develop); 'tag I compute  : ' + (Get-Content VERSION) + '-' + (git rev-parse --short develop); 'tag of the build: ' + $tag; Select-String -Path Jenkinsfile -Pattern 'env.IMAGE_TAG|env.GIT_SHORT' | Select-Object -First 2 | ForEach-Object { $_.Line.Trim() }
steps.expect: Version 1.1.0, commit 1c2103c (or the current one), and the same tag 1.1.0-1c2103c computed two ways, plus the two Jenkinsfile lines that build it.
steps.tell: Every image carries the version and the commit it was built from.

steps.title: Build and push, as recorded in the Jenkins log
steps.say: Now the Jenkins log. Docker build creates the application image with the registry prefix and the tag, and passes the version and the commit as build arguments. Then docker push publishes it to the local registry, and the registry answers with a digest, a unique fingerprint of the image. The same happens for the Nginx image.
steps.cmd: (Invoke-WebRequest 'http://localhost:8090/job/hotel-booking/lastBuild/consoleText' -Headers $jh -UseBasicParsing).Content -split '\r?\n' | Select-String '\+ docker build -|\+ docker push|digest:' | ForEach-Object { $_.Line -replace '^\[[^\]]+\]\s*', '' }
steps.expect: Two 'docker build -t localhost:5000/hotel-booking-...' lines with the build arguments, two 'docker push' lines and the two digests (sha256:...).
steps.tell: The log shows the images built with the version and commit and pushed to the registry.

steps.title: The local registry and all published releases
steps.say: The registry itself. I ask it directly, over its HTTP interface, which repositories it holds: the application and Nginx. And which tags the application has: every release that the pipeline ever published, version and commit. The new one is among them. These older tags are also the candidates for a rollback, because nothing has to be rebuilt.
steps.expect: hotel-booking-app and hotel-booking-nginx, and eight tags such as 1.0.0-64351fe ... 1.1.0-1c2103c.
steps.tell: The registry keeps every published release, which makes rollback possible.

steps.title: The commit is inside the image
steps.say: The image carries its own identity. I inspect the image from the registry tag and print its labels. The revision label holds the commit id, and the version label the version. These labels are written at build time from the build arguments. So even without Jenkins, anyone can ask an image which commit it was built from.
steps.expect: org.opencontainers.image.revision = the commit (1c2103c), org.opencontainers.image.version = 1.1.0, title hotel-booking-app.
steps.tell: Each image carries the commit and version it was built from, as labels.

steps.title: Deployment: a fresh container
steps.say: Deployment. Jenkins runs docker compose pull, which fetches the images that were just published, then docker compose up with the wait option. Look at the log: the staging app container was recreated, started, and Docker reported it healthy, then the Nginx container as well. It was recreated because the new image has a new identity. The database stays safe, because it lives in a separate volume.
steps.expect: '+ docker compose pull', '+ docker compose up -d --no-build --wait ...', 'Container hotel-staging-app-1 Recreated / Started / Healthy' and 'Deployed 1.1.0-... to staging: http://localhost:8081'.
steps.tell: The pipeline pulled the tested image and started a fresh container, waiting until it was healthy.

steps.title: The running container is the published image
steps.say: Is the container running the image that was tested and published? I compare two image ids. The first is the image the running staging container was created from. The second is the image behind the tag in the registry. They are identical, character for character. The tested image became the deployed release, with no rebuild in between. The container list shows both staging containers, healthy.
steps.cmd: docker ps --filter name=hotel-staging --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}'; 'running container image id: ' + (docker inspect hotel-staging-app-1 --format '{{.Image}}'); 'registry tag image id     : ' + (docker image inspect "localhost:5000/hotel-booking-app:$tag" --format '{{.Id}}')
steps.expect: hotel-staging-app-1 and hotel-staging-nginx-1 Up (healthy), staging port 8081, and two identical sha256 image ids.
steps.tell: The container runs exactly the image that Jenkins tested and published.

steps.title: Health verification: version and commit
steps.say: Finally the health verification. I ask the running staging application for its health: status ok, environment staging, the version, and the commit. I compare the commit with the tip of develop, and with the health file that the pipeline itself saved during its health check stage. All the same. The deployed version is traceable to one commit and one Jenkins build.
steps.cmd: curl.exe -s http://localhost:8081/health; ''; 'commit at the tip of develop: ' + (git rev-parse --short develop); 'health.json saved by Jenkins:'; Invoke-RestMethod 'http://localhost:8090/job/hotel-booking/lastBuild/artifact/reports/health.json' -Headers $jh | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
steps.expect: {"commit":"1c2103c","env":"staging","status":"ok","version":"1.1.0"}, the same commit as develop, and the same JSON in health.json.
steps.tell: The deployed version and commit match the build, so the release is verified and traceable.

steps.title: Docker Hub: the honest status
steps.say: I must be honest about Docker Hub. The pipeline supports it: if the registry parameter does not start with localhost, it logs in with a Jenkins credential called registry creds, and the password is masked in the log. These are the lines. But I never ran it, because it needs a Docker Hub account and an access token. Everything shown in this video used the local registry. To publish externally I would set the registry parameter to docker dot io slash my id and add the credential in Jenkins. I will not publish anything or store credentials without your authorization.
steps.expect: The REGISTRY parameter, the startsWith('localhost') test, withCredentials registry-creds and the docker login line.
steps.tell: Docker Hub publishing is implemented but untested; the local registry was used and verified.
